newsitem.title: FRANCE: French immigration bill sparks protest march.
newsitem.headline: French immigration bill sparks protest march.

text.p: Several thousand demonstrators marched through Paris on Sunday to demand the withdrawal of a controversial immigration bill intended to shut loopholes in already tough existing laws.

Leftist movements, including the Socialist and Communist parties, backed the march called by anti-racism groups, trade unions and intellectuals ahead of a final reading debate in the Senate on Tuesday.
Organisers said 30,000 to 40,000 people took part, but police put the number at 11,000, slightly less than a previous demonstration on February 24. Demonstrations in provincial cities were smaller.
About 300 people protested in Lille in France's northern industrial heartland where a dozen Asian and African immigrants hvae been on hunger strike for the past 55 days to demand residence papers.
In Toulouse in southern France, only about 50 protesters turned out on a city square, witnesses said.

"We are here to sound the alarm bell once again," Mouloud Aounit, of the anti-racism MRAP movement, said after the bill's passage through the National Assembly last month prompted protests from film-makers and artists.
The bill would grant extended powers to police to track immigrants and would set up records of visitors staying in France.
One key article would authorise police to keep the passports or travel documents of illegal immigrants and allow searches of commercial vehicles within 20 km (12 miles) of the border.
The bill would also authorise police to take the fingerprints of foreigners from outside the European Union who apply for a residence permit.

The ruling Gaullist RPR party dismissed Sunday's protest, saying the turnout when the Socialists had called for participation highlighted "the divide separating Socialist gestures and the concerns of the French people."
"This is a new blow for the Socialists' credibility," the party said in a statement.

The Socialists' number two, Daniel Vaillant, took part in the march with Socialist former labour minister Martine Aubry. The party had dithered for days before jumping on the bandwaggon launched by artists and intellectuals.
"Immigration is not the country's chief problem," said writer Dan Franck. "The authorities should do their job rather than designate scapegoats."

Franck was among hundreds of artists, lawyers and writers who signed petitions urging the French to disobey a clause in the original bill requiring people to report the departure of foreign guests to the authorities.
The bill has now been amended to order guests themselves to tell the authorities when they leave.
